sources.text:
A scheduler chooses which ready job receives the processor. Turnaround time equals completion time minus arrival time. Response time equals the first time a job runs minus its arrival time. These metrics measure different things: early access to a processor does not necessarily imply early completion. First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preempting them. Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Comparisons involving these shortest-job policies must state how execution lengths are known.

Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. Neither a smaller average response time nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes that a policy is best for every objective.

A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Jobs in higher-priority queues run before lower-priority jobs; equal-priority jobs can share service by Round Robin. New jobs begin at high priority, and consuming the allowed CPU allotment causes demotion. Accounting for total consumed allotment prevents a job from retaining high priority indefinitely merely by yielding just before each slice ends. Periodic priority boosts can help jobs otherwise left waiting at low priority. Queue levels, slice lengths, allotments, and boost intervals are policy parameters, not universal constants.

This fixture adds an explicit scheduling model for exercises. It is authored example scaffolding rather than text copied from a textbook. Unless a question states otherwise, there is one processor, jobs are independent, and each job consists of one CPU burst with no I/O. Arrival times and required CPU service are provided. The processor never serves two jobs simultaneously. Time spent switching is not CPU service delivered to any job. A job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the remaining slice. If a job arrives at exactly a slice boundary, the question must say whether that arrival is enqueued before or after the preempted job. Ties must be resolved by an explicit rule, such as alphabetical job names.

A question that includes switching overhead must define when that overhead applies: for example, only when moving between different jobs, with no initial dispatch charge. It must also state whether arrivals can occur while switching and how they enter the queue. Questions that ignore overhead must say so. These conventions make a timeline reproducible and prevent a numeric answer from depending on unstated simulator behavior.

A comparison can report each job's first-run and completion times, then compute the requested averages. A design recommendation also needs an objective and constraints, such as a maximum response time, a switching budget, or a fairness requirement. A policy can satisfy one constraint while losing on another metric. Choosing a scheduler should therefore follow the stated workload and requirements. response.evidence_note: The supplied fixture defines response time, turnaround time, Round Robin mechanics, switching overhead conventions, and the single-processor non-I/O model; these are sufficient to author one hard short-answer scheduling-design question with numerical analysis. No external workload trace is required.
learning_objectives: Compute per-job response time and turnaround time from a given arrival/service workload and a fully specified scheduler configuration.
Distinguish the objectives served by small versus large time slices and by RR versus STCF.
Justify a scheduler recommendation against explicit constraints such as a maximum response time and a switching budget.

sections.heading: Model and Conventions for This Exercise
sections.text: Assume one processor; jobs are independent, each with a single CPU burst and no I/O. Arrival times and required CPU service are given. Time spent switching is not CPU service delivered to any job; initial dispatch is free. Round Robin (RR) runs each selected job for at most one time slice, then moves an unfinished job to the back of the ready queue. A job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the remaining slice; simultaneous arrivals are ordered by id lexicographic order. For STCF, the running job is preempted whenever another available job has strictly less remaining time; ties in remaining time use id order. These conventions are taken from the fixture and must be used in your calculation.

sections.heading: Reading Response and Turnaround Time
sections.text: Turnaround time equals completion time minus arrival time. Response time equals the first time a job runs minus its arrival time. Early access to the processor does not necessarily imply early completion: a job may first run quickly under a short slice but still complete late if it is repeatedly preempted. Metrics must therefore be reported per job and not collapsed to a single number when comparing policies.

questions.stem:
Workload: four independent single-burst jobs arrive as follows, with all times in integer abstract units.

| Job | Arrival | CPU service needed |
|-----|---------|--------------------|
| A   | 0       | 7                  |
| B   | 1       | 3                  |
| C   | 4       | 2                  |
| D   | 6       | 1                  |

You must compare two policies for this workload.

Policy RR: one time slice q = 2. Switching overhead applies only when the processor moves between different jobs. After any switch, the next job starts at the end of the switch cost. Arrivals during a switch are appended to the tail of the ready queue. A job in a low-priority queue may be boosted periodically, but for this problem no boosts occur. Assume that a job finishing before its slice expires does not consume the unused remainder, and that initial dispatch is free. For the overhead cases, use switch cost c = 3, and use c = 0 only to show the no-overhead RR baseline.

Policy STCF: preemptive shortest time-to-completion first with no switching overhead; the running job is preempted only if another available job has strictly less remaining time; break equal-remaining-time ties by id lexicographic order. When the running job is preempted or completes, the newly selected job starts immediately.

Answer ALL of the following parts. Show enough intermediate timeline detail to justify each number.

(a) Using RR with q = 2 and c = 0, give the first-run and completion times for every job, then compute (i) average response time and (ii) average turnaround time over the four jobs.

(b) Repeat part (a) using the same RR q = 2 but with c = 3. State clearly at which times switching overhead is charged and which job runs when.

(c) Using STCF with no switching overhead, give the first-run and completion times for every job, and compute average response time and average turnaround time.

(d) A design team says: "We want the smallest possible average response time, and we also want to keep the number of switches small; therefore we should use the smallest RR slice that keeps average response time minimal." Test this reasoning against your computed values. Does a smaller slice necessarily improve average turnaround time here? Does the no-overhead RR result at q = 2 outperform STCF on both metrics, or only on one? Explain using the jobs and constraints above.

(e) Recommend one concrete scheduler configuration from the options you evaluated, or from a justified adjustment within the RR parameters you may state. Your recommendation must include: (i) a policy with q and c, (ii) whether it meets the explicit constraint "average response time no greater than the best value you computed," and (iii) whether it meets the explicit constraint "no more than a modest switching count." If no single evaluated option satisfies both constraints, say so and justify the closest feasible compromise. Your answer must refer to the actual arrival/service numbers and to the response versus turnaround distinction.
questions.answer:
(a) RR with q=2, c=0, ready queue FIFO, arrivals at boundaries enqueued before preempted job (boundary=before). Timeline: A[0-2], B[2-4], A[4-6], C[6-8], D[8-9], B[9-10], A[10-11]. First run: A=0, B=2, C=6, D=8. Completion: A=11, B=10, C=8, D=9. Response times (first run minus arrival): A=0, B=1, C=2, D=2; average = 1.25. Turnaround times (completion minus arrival): A=11, B=9, C=4, D=3; average = 6.75.

(b) RR with q=2, c=3, switch cost charged only between different jobs; transitions A→B, B→A, A→C, C→D, D→B, B→A each cost 3. Timeline: A[0-2], switch 2-5, B[5-7], switch 7-10, A[10-12], switch 12-15, C[15-17], switch 17-20, D[20-21] finishes, switch 21-24, B[24-26], switch 26-29, A[29-31]. First run: A=0, B=5, C=15, D=20. Completion: A=31, B=26, C=17, D=21. Response times: A=0, B=4, C=11, D=14; average = 7.25. Turnaround times: A=31, B=25, C=13, D=15; average = 21.00. Switch count = 6.

(c) STCF with no overhead: at t=0 A runs. At t=1 B arrives with remaining 3 < A remaining 6, so B runs. At t=4 B completes, C arrives with remaining 2 < A remaining 6, so C runs. At t=6 C completes, D arrives with remaining 1 < A remaining 6, so D runs. D completes at t=7; A resumes and runs 7-13. First run: A=0, B=1, C=4, D=6. Completion: A=13, B=4, C=6, D=7. Response times: A=0, B=0, C=0, D=0; average = 0. Turnaround times: A=13, B=3, C=2, D=1; average = 4.75.

(d) The reasoning is partly wrong. A smaller RR slice can reduce initial response time because more jobs get a first turn earlier, but it increases switch frequency and can raise turnaround time when switch cost is charged. Here c=0 RR q=2 gives average response 1.25, while c=3 RR q=2 gives 7.25; STCF gives average response 0 and average turnaround 4.75. So STCF beats c=0 RR q=2 on both measured metrics, not only one. The claim that smaller slices keep average turnaround minimal is not supported by this workload. The claim that switching count should be kept small is reasonable, but the numerical comparison shows that response-time improvement and switching reduction are separate objectives and can conflict.

(e) A defensible recommendation is STCF with c=0 for this workload. It satisfies the response-time constraint: its average response time is 0, which is no greater than the best value computed (also 0). Its switching count under the fixture's STCF model is 0 adjacent different-process transitions, so it satisfies a modest-switching constraint. If the design requires RR only, then RR q=2 c=0 gives average response 1.25 and average turnaround 6.75, but it does not match STCF on either metric; larger q would reduce switching frequency but may worsen response time, and c=3 is much worse on average response than STCF. If no RR configuration can meet both explicit constraints while keeping switching low, the evaluator should say so and choose the closest feasible compromise: STCF is the closest because it has both the best response time and zero switching overhead in this model. The response versus turnaround distinction matters because STCF's first runs occur at arrivals 1, 4, and 6 for B, C, and D, giving zero response for all three non-A jobs, while RR's first runs are delayed by queue rotation and switching overhead, and its turnaround values are larger than STCF's.
questions.explanation: For RR q=2 c=0, the timeline is A, B, A, C, D, B, A. Each unfinished job goes to the back after its slice. First-run times are read directly from the timeline; completion times are the last time each job runs. Then response = first run minus arrival, turnaround = completion minus arrival. For RR with c=3, every different-job transition costs 3 units before the next job can run. For STCF, a running job is preempted only if another available job has strictly less remaining time; here B preempts A at t=1, C at t=4, and D at t=6, so the shortest jobs finish first and A completes last. This yields the STCF values. The design reasoning fails because smaller slices and zero overhead are not the same thing: the c=3 case shows that switch cost can dominate the response-time benefit, while STCF avoids both the rotation delay and the switch overhead in this model.

sections.heading: Scheduling metrics and conventions
sections.text: Turnaround time = completion time minus arrival time; response time = first time a job runs minus its arrival time. These are distinct: a job may start early but finish late. Round Robin runs each selected job for at most one time slice before requeuing any unfinished job at the back; shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but raise context-switch frequency, and larger slices amortize switches but lengthen waits before a different job first runs. STCF is preemptive and picks the job with least remaining service time. For reproducibility, a timeline must fix: the preemption boundary rule, whether an arrival at a slice edge is enqueued before or after the preempted job, whether switching overhead applies and when, and the tie-breaking rule.

questions.stem:
Consider four independent single-burst jobs on one processor with no I/O. Arrivals and required CPU service (in abstract time units) are: A arrives at 0 with burst 7; B arrives at 1 with burst 3; C arrives at 4 with burst 2; D arrives at 6 with burst 1. Ties are broken by lexicographic job id. Assume a job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the rest of the slice, and initial dispatch and dispatch after an idle interval are free.

(a) Using Round Robin with quantum = 2 and zero switch cost, list each job's first-start time, completion time, response time, and turnaround time, then give the average response time and average turnaround time.

(b) Now assume a switch cost of 3 time units that is charged only when the processor moves between two different jobs (no initial dispatch charge). During a switch, arrivals are appended to the tail of the ready queue, and the next job is selected before the switch begins. Using Round Robin with quantum = 2, list the full timeline (including switch intervals) and each job's first-start time, completion time, response time, and turnaround time, plus the average response and average turnaround times.

(c) Using STCF (preemptive, zero switch cost), list the full timeline and each job's completion time, then give average response and average turnaround.

(d) Compare (a), (b), and (c) on average response time and average turnaround time, and state which metric each policy wins on for this workload.

(e) A designer wants both a low average response time and a bounded switching overhead on this workload. Recommend either RR (with one of the quanta/costs above) or STCF, and justify the recommendation by explicitly citing the metric values and constraints you computed. Explain one way in which the recommendation could change if the stated objective were turnaround time only.
questions.answer:
(a) RR q=2, c=0: Timeline A[0,2], B[2,4], A[4,6], C[6,8], B[8,9], D[9,10], A[10,13]. First starts: A=0, B=2, C=6, D=9. Completions: A=13, B=9, C=8, D=10. Response times: A=0, B=1, C=2, D=3 → average response = 6/4 = 1.5. Turnaround times: A=13, B=8, C=4, D=4 → average turnaround = 29/4 = 7.25.

(b) RR q=2, c=3, switch charged only between different jobs, arrivals appended to tail during switching, next job chosen before the switch: Timeline A[0,2], switch[2,5], B[5,7], switch[7,10], A[10,12], switch[12,15], C[15,17], switch[17,20], D[20,21], B[21,22], A[22,25]. First starts: A=0, B=5, C=15, D=20. Completions: A=25, B=22, C=17, D=21. Response times: A=0, B=4, C=11, D=14 → average response = 29/4 = 7.25. Turnaround times: A=25, B=21, C=13, D=15 → average turnaround = 74/4 = 18.5.

(c) STCF (c=0): Timeline A[0,1], B[1,4], C[4,6], D[6,7], A[7,13]. At t=1, B (remaining 3) preempts A (remaining 6); at t=2, B still has less remaining than A, so B continues. Completions: A=13, B=4, C=6, D=7. First starts: A=0, B=1, C=4, D=6. Response times: A=0, B=0, C=0, D=0 → average response = 0. Turnaround times: A=13, B=3, C=2, D=1 → average turnaround = 19/4 = 4.75.

(d) Average response: STCF (0) < RR c=0 (1.5) < RR c=3 (7.25). STCF wins on response. Average turnaround: STCF (4.75) < RR c=0 (7.25) < RR c=3 (18.5). STCF also wins on turnaround for this workload; RR c=0 is the better of the two RR variants.

(e) Recommendation: choose STCF. On this workload it already yields average response = 0 and average turnaround = 4.75 with zero switching cost, so it dominates RR c=0 (1.5, 7.25) and RR c=3 (7.25, 18.5) on both metrics, and it does not need the 12 units of switching overhead that RR c=3 incurs. If the sole objective were turnaround time, STCF still wins here (4.75 vs 7.25 and 18.5), so the recommendation would not change for this specific workload; the choice could only change if additional constraints (e.g., unknown or highly variable burst lengths, or a requirement to favor short jobs' responsiveness while punishing long jobs) were introduced, since STCF's advantage relies on known or well-predicted service times, whereas RR with a small slice is preferable when burst lengths are unknown and the goal is predominantly interactive responsiveness.
questions.explanation: Application of the fixture's definitions: turnaround = completion − arrival, response = first run − arrival. The RR c=0 timeline follows FIFO requeuing after each 2-unit slice. The RR c=3 timeline inserts 3-unit switches only between different jobs and appends arrivals during switching to the tail. The STCF timeline consistently re-evaluates remaining time at each arrival; B (remaining 3) preempts A (remaining 6) at t=1 and, at t=2, still has less remaining (2 vs 5), so it continues to t=4. STCF therefore gives each job its first run at or before the next arrival, producing zero response time.
